why: Recommend: ask. Not literally --force, -f or +refspec, but it still rewrites the default branch's history; the lease only stops it clobbering remote work you have not fetched. Same for --force-if-includes.
Recommend: ask. --mirror force-updates (and deletes) every remote ref, the default branch included, without any force flag.
Recommend: allow in L7b (deleting is not a force push), list it as a G4.1a candidate. Same question for the refspec form git push origin :main.
Recommend: allow. Nothing is sent; consistent with git push -n (spa-051) and Remove-Item -WhatIf (spa-033). Asking would also be harmless.

Recommend: allow when default_branch is known (here it is main, so master is an ordinary branch). Only fall back to treating both main and master as default when the default branch cannot be resolved.
Recommend: block (ask). -n is git commit's documented short form of --no-verify (also bundled, e.g. -nm). On git push, -n means --dry-run, so it must stay allowed there (spa-051).
Recommend: ask for a core.hooksPath override on commit or push (same effect as --no-verify); allow tool-specific switches such as HUSKY=0 or SKIP=... in L7b. Literally outside the family.
Recommend: allow in L7b (the family names git commit and git push only), G4.1a candidate. Same for git rebase --no-verify and git am --no-verify, which also skip hooks.
Recommend: allow (it is configuration, not a commit). Gap: a later git cnv is invisible to a text policy; doctor could list git aliases that contain --no-verify.
Recommend: block. git accepts any unambiguous prefix of a long option, so --no-verif is --no-verify. Unlikely from an agent, which is why it is not gated.

Recommend: allow (literal reading). In the Vite/Next convention .env.production, .env.development and .env.test are committed defaults and the .local variants hold secrets. Risk: some projects keep real secrets in .env.production; the owner may prefer ask.
Recommend: ask. The agent's own shell reads the file and any later command in the chain can print the values. Same for '. .env' and 'set -a; source .env'.
Recommend: allow. A program loads the file; its contents do not reach the transcript. Same for docker compose --env-file .env and dotenv run. Asking here would fire on every dev-server start.
Recommend: allow (metadata only, no contents). Same for test -f .env, Test-Path .env and git check-ignore -v .env, which agents run to confirm .env is ignored.
Recommend: block (ask). The glob matches .env and .env.local whenever they exist; a text policy cannot see the file system, so it should assume they do.
Recommend: ask. A backup (.bak, .old, .backup, .orig) carries the same secrets as .env, but the literal list does not include it.
Recommend: block. It matches .env.*.local literally, and the exemption names three exact file names. A .local file is gitignored and can hold real values.
Recommend: block on Windows and macOS (case-insensitive file systems, so .ENV is .env); exact-case match on Linux.
Recommend: allow. Here .env is a Python virtualenv folder (python -m venv .env); the file read is .env/bin/activate, not a dotenv file. Match the last path segment, not any segment.
Recommend: allow, and document the gap. A recursive grep reads .env without naming it; so do tar, zip and git add -A. A text policy cannot see this.
Recommend: block. It prints a committed .env from history; the path sits after the colon of a revision spec.
Recommend: ask. The edit reads the file but prints nothing; a text policy cannot reliably tell an in-place edit from a read (sed without -i prints).
Recommend: block (ask). It is a read; keeping a list of readers that never print content (wc, sha256sum, file) invites misses.
Recommend: allow (the file name is app.env, not .env). Docker env_file files named *.env often hold secrets; G4.1a candidate.

Recommend: ask. In bash a quoted ~ is not expanded, so this removes a folder literally named ~ in cwd (often created by a tool bug). Asking costs one prompt; a near miss here is the classic way people delete their home. Same for "~" and '$HOME'.
Recommend: block. $PWD is cwd, which is the project root here; the plan's expansion list names only home variables. Same for "$(pwd)" and PowerShell $PWD or (Get-Location).

Recommend: block if the policy tracks cd within a chain (the definition covers it: this deletes the project root). It is not gated because resolving it needs cd tracking; spb-020, spb-045 and spb-060 only chain after cd.
Recommend: block. Deleting an ancestor deletes the project root with it. Same for ancestors of home: /home, /Users, C:\Users.
Recommend: allow in L7b (the family covers home, roots and the project root only); top-level system folders (/etc, /usr, /bin, C:\Windows) are a G4.1a candidate.
Recommend: block. find -delete with no filter on home or / is a recursive delete by another command (find / -delete as well).
Recommend: allow (the variable is not one the plan expands). If OUT_DIR is unset this is rm -rf /*; the owner may want ask when the variable is unset in the hook's environment.
Recommend: block. ~dev expands to dev's home folder, which is the home here; it needs a user lookup or a match on the last segment of home.
Recommend: block. Git Bash inherits the Windows environment, so $USERPROFILE is the home folder; the plan lists %USERPROFILE% and $env:USERPROFILE but not the bash form.
Recommend: block. It expands to the home folder; likewise %SystemDrive%\ and $env:SystemDrive\ expand to a drive root. Not in the plan's expansion list.

Recommend: block. A drive letter without a slash means the current folder on that drive, which is the project root here; a policy that reads C: as the drive root also asks, so either reading gives the same answer.

Recommend: block. In Windows PowerShell -rf is not a Remove-Item parameter, so it errors and deletes nothing; but it is the plan's own example text, asking is harmless, and in pwsh on Linux or macOS rm is /bin/rm.
Recommend: block. A pipeline that feeds every child of a drive root (or home) into a recursive Remove-Item deletes it as surely as a path argument.

Recommend: block (parse the eval string like bash -c). Deeper indirection (echo ~ | xargs rm -rf, a target held in a variable set earlier, base64 | sh) is out of reach of an accident gate; document it rather than gate it.
Recommend: allow (not recursive, so outside the family), though it deletes every top-level file in home. Folders survive.
Recommend: block, for consistency with /* and ~/* in must-block (it empties the project root). Same for Remove-Item -Recurse -Force .\* and rd/del on .\*.
